claims.text: Sputter-depositing an ultra-thin HEA coating followed by post-deposition annealing around 700°C will improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of zirconium-alloy cladding.
The coating and annealing treatment will induce formation of a stabilized multi-element oxide barrier.
The intervention will preserve the mechanical and thermal properties required for reactor service.
Post-deposition annealing relieves stresses in the sputtered coating.
The HEA's multicomponent structure facilitates in situ formation of multiple low-diffusivity oxide particles.
The oxide particles merge into a continuous, adherent surface barrier.
During high-temperature exposure, diverse oxide phases in the HEA coalesce into a dense, slow-growing oxide scale.
The dense oxide scale impedes oxygen diffusion into the zirconium-alloy substrate.
The oxide scale maintains good adhesion and minimizes spallation during high-temperature exposure.
HEA-coated cladding will have a substantially lower oxidation rate than uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding under comparable high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
HEA-coated cladding will have a substantially lower oxidation rate than conventionally coated cladding under comparable high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
HEA-coated cladding will retain mechanical integrity better than uncoated or conventionally coated cladding.
Uncoated or conventionally coated zirconium-alloy cladding will oxidize faster under similar high-temperature conditions.
Uncoated or conventionally coated zirconium-alloy cladding will undergo earlier mechanical degradation under similar high-temperature conditions.
The protective effect is expected to hold during exposure to oxidizing environments above 1000°C when controlled sputter-deposition and annealing conditions are used.
Scaling the optimized coating process to complex cladding geometries may make it difficult to maintain uniform coating integrity.
Long-term performance and coating uniformity on complex surfaces remain uncertain.
